summary: Defines a new SIP Via header field parameter, received-realm, which lets an entry point to a transit network record which adjacent upstream network a request came from.

eli5.summary: Like a postmark saying which post office a letter came from, this tag tells which neighboring network sent a call request.

questions: what is the sip received-realm parameter
how does a transit network identify the upstream network
what claims are in the received-realm jws
how to verify received-realm in sip
subtitle: A signed tag in the SIP Via header that tells a transit network which neighbouring network a call request came from.

tldr.problem: A transit network that carries SIP requests for many other networks often needs to know which adjacent upstream network sent each request, to apply the right services or routing policy. An Inter Operator Identifier cannot be used because it is not defined for enterprise networks.
tldr.mechanism: The network entry point adds a received-realm parameter to its Via header field. It holds an operator identifier plus a detached JSON Web Signature over values taken from the request, so other nodes in the operator's network can verify it.
tldr.outcome: Nodes inside the transit network can trust the parameter, as long as they verify the signature and the parameter was inserted by an entity able to verify the upstream network.

facts.label: Separator in the value
facts.value: colon between operator identifier and JWS

today: RFC 8055 is a Proposed Standard, published in January 2017, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the received-realm Via parameter.

sections.title: Why a Transit Network Needs to Know
sections.content:
When SIP sessions cross networks belonging to different operators, or interconnected networks of the same operator or enterprise, the requests might traverse transit networks. To offer its services, a transit network often needs to know to which operator or enterprise the adjacent upstream network belongs. This RFC adds a Via header field parameter, received-realm, for that purpose.

The text gives two use cases. In the first, an Application Server in a transit IMS network provides services per served network rather than per user, so it must know which upstream network the request arrived from. In the second, a transit routing entity applies a set of routing policies defined for each customer, so it must know which customer sent the request.

An Inter Operator Identifier (IOI) cannot be used here, because IOIs are not defined for enterprise networks.
sections.eli5: A big sorting office handles mail from many towns. To treat each town's mail properly, it needs to know which town each bag came from.

sections.title: Where the Mechanism Applies
sections.content:
The mechanism MUST only be used by SIP entities that are able to verify from which adjacent upstream network a request was received. How to verify this is outside the scope of the RFC. It gives examples: receiving the request on an authenticated Virtual Private Network, on a specific IP address, or on a specific network access.

The document defines a network entry point as a SIP entity on the border of the network that receives requests from adjacent upstream networks. It defines the adjacent upstream SIP network as the adjacent network in the direction from which a request is received.
sections.eli5: Only a doorman who can really tell which town a visitor came from is allowed to write that down.

sections.title: The received-realm Parameter
sections.content:
The parameter value is a quoted string made of two parts separated by a colon: an operator identifier and a serialized JSON Web Signature (JWS, RFC 7515). The operator identifier is a token that represents the adjacent operator. Its scope is only within the network that inserts it, and it is case insensitive.

The JWS payload is not carried in the header. It is built from values found elsewhere in the SIP message, so the payload is detached as described in Appendix F of RFC 7515. In the ABNF the signature is written header ".." signature, and the two adjacent dots are there because the detached payload is replaced by an empty string.
sections.eli5: The tag has a short name for the neighbouring network and a seal. The text the seal protects is not written on the tag, because the receiver can read it from the rest of the letter.

sections.title: The Signed Payload
sections.content:
The JWS header MUST include typ with the value JWT and alg with the algorithm used. Operators need to agree on the set of supported algorithms and use values registered for alg.

The payload MUST include six claims, each copied from the SIP message: sip_from_tag, sip_date, sip_callid, sip_cseq_num, sip_via_branch and sip_via_opid. Because only the sender and receiver build the payload, both must serialize it identically. All claims are lowercase, in the order just listed, and encoded as strings except sip_date, which is a JSON NumericDate. The payload follows the rules of Step 1 of Section 3 of RFC 7638.
sections.eli5: The seal covers a list of six facts about the call, always written in the same order, so the sender and receiver end up with exactly the same list.

sections.title: Who Adds and Who Checks It
sections.content:
A SIP entity acting as a network entry point adds its Via header field as usual under RFC 3261. If it can assert the adjacent upstream network and knows a network realm value for it, it can add the received-realm parameter with that value as the operator identifier. It MUST then calculate the JWS and put the header and signature in the jws part.

A SIP entity that wants to act on the value MUST first recalculate the JWS and compare it with the one received. If they do not match, it MUST discard the parameter, and it MAY also take other action such as rejecting the request, based on local policy.
sections.eli5: The doorman writes the tag and seals it. Anyone inside who wants to rely on the tag first checks the seal, and throws the tag away if the seal does not fit.

sections.title: An INVITE Through a Transit Entry Point
sections.content: The RFC shows an INVITE from a user agent in Operator 1 reaching the entry point T_EP and then an Application Server T_AS. The proxy inserts a Via header field with received-realm="myoperator:..." in the request and removes it from the response. The example operator identifier is myoperator and the example algorithm is HS256.
sections.eli5: The tag is stuck on when the letter enters the sorting office and peeled off again when the reply leaves.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the parameter can trigger applications, it must not be added by an unauthorized SIP entity. It is inserted, signed, verified and consumed within one operator network. The operator MUST discard parameters received from another network, and only entities able to verify the upstream network may insert it.

The key used for the signature should be known only to the entities that sign or verify. The operator MUST use a key management policy that protects stored keys against unauthorized access and against cryptanalysis using captured data sent on the wire. A SIP entity MUST NOT use the adjacent network information if the received and calculated signatures differ. Generic JWS security considerations are in RFC 7515.
sections.eli5: Only trusted staff may hold the seal stamp, and any tag from outside the building is thrown away.
